what: CSW Industrials makes and distributes specialised products for contractors, chiefly in heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration and plumbing. Its RectorSeal business sells thread sealants, condensate pumps, line-set covers, mini-split accessories and chemicals that HVAC and plumbing installers use every day. Smaller businesses make engineered railings and building products, and specialised lubricants and sealants for industrial and rail customers.
customers: HVAC/R and plumbing contractors buying through wholesale distributors, plus building owners, architects and industrial customers in mining, rail and energy.
money: HVAC/R, plumbing and electrical products sold through distributors, many under the RectorSeal brand.
Architectural railings, smoke vents and building products.
Industrial lubricants, sealants and reliability products.
moat: Its products are small-ticket items that a contractor buys by brand name and that make up a tiny share of a job’s cost, so price matters far less than availability and familiarity. Distributors stock CSW’s broad catalogue because contractors ask for it, which gives the company high gross margins of about 42% and lets it roll up smaller niche brands and push them through the same shelf space.
risks: The shares trade at about 37 times trailing earnings and 20 times EV/EBITDA, leaving little room for disappointment.
Net income fell from $137M to $112M in fiscal 2026 despite a 23% rise in revenue, as acquisition costs, interest and weaker residential HVAC demand bit.
Debt has risen to $847M against $37M of cash after recent acquisitions.
Residential HVAC volumes are cyclical and were disrupted by the refrigerant transition and distributor destocking.
Growth depends on continuing to find and integrate acquisitions at sensible prices.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $626M in fiscal 2022 to $1.25B over the last twelve months, helped by acquisitions such as Aspen Manufacturing.
Forward earnings of about 24 times look more reasonable if margins recover from the acquisition costs.
Each acquired brand can be sold through CSW’s existing distribution relationships, which is where the roll-up creates value.
Ageing US HVAC equipment and the shift to heat pumps and mini-splits create steady demand for installation accessories.
watch: Organic growth in Contractor Solutions, margins of recent acquisitions, debt reduction and any recovery in residential HVAC volumes.
view: CSW is a quality compounder that has been priced as one for a long time, and the last year exposed the gap between that price and the earnings. Its RectorSeal products are the definition of a good niche business: cheap, essential, bought by habit and sold through distributors who carry the whole range. That is why gross margin sits around 42% and why the company has been able to buy similar brands and grow them through the same channel.

The fiscal 2026 numbers are the test. Revenue rose 23% to $1.08B, largely from acquisitions, but net income fell 18% to $112M as interest on new debt, integration costs and weak residential HVAC volumes ate into margins. Debt went from almost nothing to $847M. None of this breaks the model, but it shows the organic engine is slower than the headline growth, and that the roll-up is now doing more of the work.

At 37 times trailing and roughly 24 times forward earnings, you are paying for a full recovery in margins and HVAC volumes. I think the business deserves a premium multiple, but this is not the moment of maximum value: I would wait for evidence that the acquired businesses are reaching CSW’s historic margins and that debt is coming down before paying this price.
bull: HVAC demand recovers, Aspen and other acquisitions reach group margins, and earnings grow into the multiple quickly.
bear: Residential HVAC stays weak and integration drags on, leaving a highly rated stock with falling earnings and higher debt.
